newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: INTERVIEW - Argentine water firm seeks compensation.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Argentine water firm seeks compensation.

text.p: Water firm Aguas Argentinas, operated by France's Lyonnaise des Eaux-Dumez, ia holding talks with the Argentine government seeking compensation for charges Aguas stopped billing at the administration's request, Aguas Director General Guy Canavy said.
The government last year asked Aguas Argentinas to stop charging clients $500 each in infrastructure costs in addition to fees for regular water service.
"The government asked us to suspend the charge, which cost us between $30 to $40 million in 1996 and would cost us about $50 million this year," he told Reuters in a weekend interview.
"We have started to discuss how to get compensation for us not charging the infrastructure payment."

A decree signed by President Carlos Menem last week allowed the modification of the 30-year concession with Aguas Argentinas, which provides water service to the greater Buenos Aires area, to start negotiations.
The talks could entail the extension of the concession contract, investment deferrals, redefinition of works and the incorporation of new areas, the decree said.
"The company's expectations are to urgently solve the charge issue that arose last year," Canavy said.
Canavy said compensatory options include charging a small part of the infrastructure rate, and then redefining some investment targets and environmental requirements.
"Probably the alternative to be chosen will be that the company suspend the net factor of about $300, and keep charging the connection, which is some $200," he said.
The net factor is a payment due to the company for the mere availability of the network.
"Some expansion plans initially marked for two to three years could be deferred over five to six years and also the construction of a fourth sewer system could be delayed."

The company said the government has asked it to accelerate the expansion of its sewer network, initially envisaged for the next 10 years in the Matanza-Riachuelo area in Buenos Aires Province, one of the country's most densely populated.

Canavy said since taking charge of water services in 1993 after the privatization of Obras Sanitarias de la Nacion, Aguas Argentinas has invested $800 million out of $1-$1.2 billion it deemed necessary to cover mandatory works for the first five years.
He added Aguas Argentinas expects $420 million in revenues this year.

Lyonnaise operates three groups in Argentina and its total clients in the country could climb to 12 million -- a third of the population -- if Aguas Cordobesas, one of the consortia it heads, were awarded the concession in Cordoba, he added.

Separately, Aguas Cordobesas vowed to invest in Cordoba $500 million over 30 years, of which $130-$150 million would be spent in the first five years. It also pledges to absorb more than 300 provincial water employees if it won the contract.

After one company withdrew, Aguas Cordobesas is the only bidder remaining for the 30-year concession. Cordoba Governor Ramon Mestre has publicly endorsed the Aguas offer. The winner will be announced in May.
